the present paper describes the association between holoprosencecephaly and hydronecephalus and chromosome 7 abnormalities in three families, including two cases of balanced chromosome rearrangements and one case of unbalanced translocation.
(i) the association between del(7q34----qter) or del(7q36----qter) and HPE was confirmed in two additional cases, and (ii) balanced rearrangements in the 7q34 region may be a new risk factor for HPE.

the presence of balanced rearrangements in mothers of non-karyotyper infants with holoprosencophaly and hydronecephaly is an additional indication of the association of del(7q34) and del(7)qter with HPE.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HPE and hydronphrosis are not associated with inv(7) and t(7;4) in the present two cases.
HPE may be caused by a deletion of a critical region of chromosome 7q, and the severity of the HPE phenotype may be related to the size of the deleted region.
HPE is a heterogeneous syndrome with at least three genetic mechanisms: (1) a single gene defect, (2) a gene deletion on 7q, and (3) a chromosomal abnormality involving 7q.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HPE and del (7q) are associated with a specific pattern of malformations.
del(7)(q32qter), del(7)(p21p22.2) and del(7)(pterq21) are the most common deletions associated with HPE.
HPE and del (7q) are linked and that HPE is a genetically complex trait with multiple genetic causes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of a 7q deletion in a child with holoprosencphaly and/or hydronephrosis should prompt the examination of the parents for a balanced translocation involving the same region.
the presence of del(7q), in particular, should alert the clinician to the possibility of HPE in the newborn.
the presence of HPE in a fetus should alert the clinician to look for a chromosomal anomaly in the mother, particularly for del(7q), as it may be associated with a high risk for recurrence.
